title: Animals With a Secret Glow. #1's Poison Glows in the Dark
description: Shine a UV light in the dark and some animals light up: scorpions, pink flying squirrels, the platypus, green sharks and the first glowing turtle. Number one was reported this year: a fire salamander whose poison glows for over 24 hours. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.
tags: animals that glow in the dark

scenes.say: You've walked past animals that glow in the dark. You just couldn't see it.

scenes.label: Glowing poison
scenes.say: Okay, so shine an ultraviolet light on this animal, and its skin lights up turquoise. Even its poison glows. But that one waits at the very end.
And it's Halloween week, the one time of year people actually own black lights. So let's talk about animals that secretly glow.

scenes.label: Not like fireflies
scenes.say: Here's the thing first. A firefly makes its own light with a chemical reaction. That's called bioluminescence. Today's animals do something different.

scenes.label: Biofluorescence
scenes.say: They soak up invisible ultraviolet light and send it back out as a color we can see. That trick is called biofluorescence.

scenes.label: More UV than day
scenes.say: And the strangest part? Full moonlight contains more ultraviolet and violet light than daylight. So the night is full of hidden glow.

scenes.label: 5 glowing animals
scenes.say: I'm counting down five animals that glow. Each one weirder than the last. And it gets stranger every step.

scenes.label: Stay for #1
scenes.say: Number one was named way back in 1758. Scientists studied it for centuries. And its glow was only reported this year.

scenes.label: Blue-green glow
scenes.say: Number five. The scorpion. Shine a UV flashlight on one at night, and it blazes blue-green like a toy.
Scorpions don't make that light. Something in a super thin layer of their outer shell absorbs ultraviolet and turns it into visible color.

scenes.label: Hyaline layer
scenes.say: That layer is called the hyaline layer. And here's the creepy part: scientists still haven't named the exact substance doing it.
Even moonlight bouncing off the shell can trigger the effect. So on a bright night, scorpions may be glowing faintly right now.

scenes.label: Babies don't glow
scenes.say: Now, baby scorpions and freshly molted ones don't glow at all. The shine only shows up once the new shell hardens.

scenes.label: Fossils glow too
scenes.say: And get this. Some fossil scorpions still fluoresce. The glow outlasted the animal by millions of years.
So why do they glow? One idea says the whole shell works like a light sensor, helping a scorpion find shade and hide from predators.
Other experts think it does nothing at all. It's just a side effect of their armor. Nobody has settled the debate yet.
But scorpions are cold, creepy bugs. What if I told you a fluffy mammal in North American forests glows bright pink?

scenes.label: Found by accident
scenes.say: Number four. The flying squirrel. And this one was found completely by accident, at a backyard bird feeder in Wisconsin.

scenes.label: Northland College
scenes.say: A forestry professor named Jon Martin was out at night with an ultraviolet flashlight. A flying squirrel came to eat.

scenes.label: Hot pink belly
scenes.say: He pointed the light at it, and the squirrel's belly fur lit up pink. Think about that. Hot pink, in a dark forest.

scenes.label: 135 skins
scenes.say: So his team checked one hundred thirty-five squirrel skins in museums in Minnesota and Chicago. Flying and regular squirrels.

scenes.label: All but one
scenes.say: The result? Across three species of New World flying squirrels, all but one specimen glowed pink.

scenes.label: Day squirrels: no
scenes.say: But the gray squirrels, fox squirrels and red squirrels you see in parks? Zero glow. None of them.
Here's the clue. Flying squirrels come out at night. The regular ones are busy in the daytime. Glow seems to go with darkness.
Before this, the only mammals known to fluoresce were opossums. Now the list had a second group. And it was about to get much weirder.

scenes.label: Of course it glows
scenes.say: Number three. The platypus. An egg-laying mammal with a duck bill and venomous spines. And yes, it glows too.

scenes.label: Just curious
scenes.say: The same Wisconsin team was shining UV lights on squirrel pelts at Chicago's Field Museum. Then, just out of curiosity, they tried a platypus.

scenes.label: Blue-green fur
scenes.say: Its fur glowed blue-green. The study came out in 2020 in the journal Mammalia. A duck-billed, egg-laying mammal that also glows.
Then another report backed it up. A platypus found on an Australian road also glowed under a black light. So it isn't just old museum skins.
But why would a platypus glow? It's out at night, and it closes its eyes when it swims. So it's probably not showing off to other platypuses.
One idea is camouflage. Many predators, including most birds, can see ultraviolet. Soaking it up might help a platypus stay hidden.
Or maybe it's just a leftover from ancient ancestors, like laying eggs. A trait that never went away. Here's the twist, though.
Some biologists who've studied platypuses for years were still amazed. One expert said the platypus never ceases to amaze them.
So far, everything glows under our lights. But what if an animal's whole world is already blue? Let's go deep underwater.

scenes.label: Glowing sharks
scenes.say: Number two. Sharks that glow green. Meet the swell shark and the chain catshark. Neither grows longer than about one meter.

scenes.label: 500-600 m deep
scenes.say: They live around five hundred to six hundred meters down. Down there, almost all the light left is blue.
Their skin absorbs that blue light and gives it back as green. To us it's hard to see. To another shark, it's a neon sign.

scenes.label: One color pigment
scenes.say: Here's why. Shark eyes have just one color pigment, tuned to blue and green. We have three. Mantis shrimp have twelve.

scenes.label: Shark-eye camera
scenes.say: So scientist David Gruber built a shark-eye camera with special filters, to see the reef the way a shark sees it.
And the sharks popped out, glowing with patterns. Spots and stripes that could help them recognize each other in the dark.

scenes.label: 200+ species
scenes.say: It's not rare, either. Biofluorescence is thought to occur in more than two hundred species of sharks and bony fish.

scenes.label: Out of nowhere
scenes.say: And then, one night dive near the Solomon Islands, something came out of nowhere. A turtle, glowing green and red.

scenes.label: First glowing reptile
scenes.say: It was a hawksbill sea turtle. Gruber's team was watching for crocodiles, and they found the first glowing reptile ever recorded.

scenes.label: Down nearly 90%
scenes.say: Sadly, hawksbill numbers worldwide have dropped by nearly ninety percent in recent decades. It's critically endangered.
Later, a local community let him check some young captive hawksbills. Every one of them glowed red. Why? Nobody knows yet.
Okay, so mammals, sharks, a turtle. But are you wondering about the slimy ones? Because that's where it gets wild.

scenes.label: First glowing frog
scenes.say: In 2017, scientists in Argentina found the first fluorescent frog. The polka-dot tree frog glows blue-green.

scenes.label: 18% of a full moon
scenes.say: Its glow molecules give off about eighteen percent as much visible light as a full moon. From a tiny frog.

scenes.label: 32 species tested
scenes.say: Then, in 2020, two researchers in Minnesota tested thirty-two kinds of amphibians under blue and ultraviolet light.

scenes.label: 32 out of 32
scenes.say: Every single one glowed. All thirty-two. Even their bones and urine lit up green, yellow or orange.

scenes.label: Fire salamander
scenes.say: Which brings us to number one. The fire salamander. Black and yellow, from the forests of Europe. And seriously poisonous.

scenes.label: Samandarines
scenes.say: Its skin makes toxins called samandarines. Scientists linked those toxins to its warning colors more than a century ago.
Carl Linnaeus named this species in 1758. Scientists have studied it, and its toxins, for a very long time. Everybody thought they knew it.

scenes.label: 10 of 12 glowed
scenes.say: Then a team from Barcelona and Germany shone UV light on salamanders in Catalonia, Spain. Ten out of twelve lit up in teal speckles.
The lead researcher said they could not believe how bright the glow was along its sides.

scenes.label: The poison glows
scenes.say: But here's the real shocker. The glow comes mostly from its skin glands. The same glands that ooze its poison.

scenes.label: 24+ hours
scenes.say: And once that toxic goo leaves the body, it keeps glowing for more than twenty-four hours.
Researchers think the glow might be a warning to predators, making its danger colors even louder in the dark.
Or it might help salamanders find each other on the forest floor, under moonlight full of ultraviolet.

scenes.label: Still a mystery
scenes.say: And the chemical behind it? Still unidentified. Maybe a molecule never recorded in this species, after centuries of study.
One scientist put it perfectly. Discoveries are a product of what we look for. So what else is glowing that we never checked?
If you use a UV light this Halloween, keep a respectful distance from wild animals. Don't grab, don't disturb.

scenes.label: Your pick?
scenes.say: Which glowing animal surprised you the most? The pink squirrel, the platypus, or the poison that glows? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: This Salamander's Poison Actually Glows in the Dark
short.description: Fire salamanders, platypuses and flying squirrels glow under UV light. Fire salamander poison keeps glowing for 24+ hours. Full countdown of 5 glowing animals on my channel.

scenes.say: This salamander's poison glows in the dark, and nobody noticed for centuries.
Shine ultraviolet light on a fire salamander, and teal speckles blaze along its sides. Ten out of twelve tested in Spain lit up.
The glow comes from the same skin glands that ooze its toxins. And that goo keeps glowing for more than twenty-four hours.
It's not alone. Platypus fur glows blue-green. Flying squirrels glow hot pink.
Scientists tested thirty-two kinds of amphibians. All thirty-two glowed. Even their bones.
And full moonlight carries more ultraviolet than daylight. So at night, the forest may be full of secret glow.
So next time you walk a dark forest, remember: one salamander's poison glows in the dark, and nobody noticed for centuries.
